title: How to use this book
text:
This book describes the 53 copepod species currently listed for New England, 3 of which have a full account so far.
Finding a species. Start with the keys (Identification keys) or the checklist (Checklist of species). Species accounts are grouped by order, then by family. Groups of species that are easily confused have their own pages under Common comparisons.
Reading an account. Each account opens with a summary box: authority, classification, habitat, the original description and other key literature, and links to external resources such as WoRMS. It then gives a diagnosis, illustrated morphology, collection records (with a map), and notes. Accounts marked draft or placeholder are still being written.
Names. Names follow the World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS). Where a name in common use is no longer accepted, the accepted name is given in the summary box.
Terminology. Morphological terms are explained in Copepod morphology and the glossary.

title: Identification keys
text:
Major body articulation behind the fifth pedigerous somite (between it and the genital somite); antennules long, usually 23–25 segments → Calanoida (see part)
Major body articulation between the fourth and fifth pedigerous somites → 2
Prosome clearly wider than the urosome; antennules of moderate length → Cyclopoida (see part)
Body more or less cylindrical, prosome and urosome of similar width; antennules short → Harpacticoida

title: Epischura nordenskiöldi
text:
Diagnosis
The female urosome is relatively straight, lacking the torsion seen in other species of Epischura (Figure 7.1). The fifth legs of both sexes separate it from E. massachusettsensis (Figure 7.2, Figure 7.3; see also Epischura species).

title: Epischura nordenskiöldi
text:
Morphology






Figure 7.1: Adult female. Note the relatively straight urosome, lacking the distinctive torsion present in other species of Epischura.









Figure 7.2: Adult female P5. The terminal segment bears six spines: one inner, three apical, and two outer. The outer spines are placed in the distal half of the segment, unlike in E. massachusettsensis, where spines are distributed along the entire length of the final segment.









Figure 7.3: Adult male P5. The terminal segment of the left leg is blunt and rounded, with four spines distributed along the distal half. The process on the inner surface of the first segment is prominent, with a slight curve. Its length is substantially more than the width of the segment, distinguishing it from the short digitiform process found in E. massachusettsensis males.

title: Epischura nordenskiöldi
text:
Notes
Schacht (1898) notes variation in the number of spines on the terminal segment of the female P5. The specimen in Figure 7.2 has six spines, but five are also observed.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
Antennule (A1)

The first, often long, pair of head appendages.

P5

The fifth leg; often sexually dimorphic and important in identification.

Prosome / urosome

The anterior and posterior divisions of the body, separated by the major articulation.
